utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in public session. The Chamber received a motion from the accused, which is the 17th motion submitted by the accused. I think this needs an urgent consideration, given that the accused seeks a suspension of the proceedings before the very next witness. So I wonder whether we can hear from the Prosecution on this motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is in the process, as we speak, of preparing a written response. If the Court wishes an expedited response, we can do that by whatever time-period the Court deems appropriate, and do that orally at some point that the Court designates. You just need to say the word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you can, could you respond orally right now, or is it more convenient for you to provide us with a courtesy copy by the end of this session?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me consider whether an oral response -- a supplemental oral response to an expedited written response is preferable. I'll be in touch with the person working on the motion, the response, at the moment. What I would like to do is make sure we're not conveying information to the Court in a piecemeal fashion, so that whatever oral response we may suggest embraces all the factors that would have been captured by the proposed written response. So rather than do it right now, let me engage in some communication and get back to the Court during the course of this day, and appreciating the fact that the Court wants as much information as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Given that we'll limit the time for the remaining cross-examination by the accused to two hours, the Chamber is minded to consider the motion during the first break of today. So if you can respond orally, let us know before the end of this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. We'll go into the closed session again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As I understand the Court's concern, I imagine that the Court is focused at the moment most particularly on the amount and nature of the material, which I'll addressed quickly in a moment. But before I do, just preliminarily I'd like to note that the reason for the period of time that elapsed between receipt and disclosure was not as suggested in the Defence motion, because the Prosecution was sitting on this material, but because of the unique natures of this material in two ways. Number 1, it was highly fragmented in the hard drive that was seized. It was split into thousands of individual files, with individual pages, an extremely cumbersome and time-consuming process that we're still looking at to make sure we have it as right as possible. And, number 2, there

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With respect to the nature of the material, Your Honour, I note that in the Defence motion it makes reference to certain examples, and the suggestion is that those are a small indication -- a small fraction of the vast nature of materials of that type spread throughout the collection. In fact, the Defence was provided with a highly-detailed index of the materials disclosed, with specific dates and, to the extent possible, indications of the source and title of the document and nature of the document. The example cited by the Defence come from one of the items that was more generally listed because it didn't lend itself in any way to more specific indications. That -- there are approximately eight items like that on the list that I saw that were not specifically itemised. Of those eight, only one is relatively voluminous, consisting of somewhat more than 200 pages. That's the one item from which the Defence cited. The other items, as I say, are both specified, encompass a wide time range, including periods of time not relevant to the indictment in the sense indicated by the motion, that is, either 1991, or 1996, or later, or clearly involving geographic areas or specific issues that have little to do with the specific upcoming witnesses coming up. So I hope that that information is useful to the Court. Obviously, should the Court have any additional questions, we'll be pleased to respond, and we'll try to provide even more details in our written response. I would also add that it appears to us quite a few items would have been duplicates already disclosed on the EDS because they were previously in-house, but that's a determination that's much more painstaking and we're still trying to assess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, do you have anything to say in reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, very briefly. And thank you for dealing with this matter on an urgent basis. Our concern was that some documents in this collection might deal with the State Hospital and that it might be necessary to recall Dr. Nakas if those documents were later located, and so we wanted to at least preserve our right to indicate that we need this time before he testifies. So we do appreciate that you're handling it before his testimony begins. First of all, though, this is different than our other disclosure motions that we filed before based on Rule 66(A)(ii), where the Prosecution inadvertently, perhaps, or at least despite their best efforts, was unable to locate documents that were in their collection. This was material that came into their position, that the significance of which I'm sure they realised immediately back in January of 2010. And we think that they fell short of their obligations under Rule 68 by holding on to this material as the trial began, as evidence started to be presented, and not at least alerting the Defence and the Chamber of the exculpatory nature of this material. So we think they have violated Rule 68 by the manner in which they handled that. Again, they are very cooperative with us, they do the best they can at addressing our requests, and we appreciate that, but we feel that in this instance they violated their obligations under Rule 68 by the way they handled this material, which was basically to make no notification of it, and until a few days before our two-week adjournment was over, to give us 6.000 pages of material, and expect that everything would just go merrily on, witness after witness without us having an opportunity to review the material. And, as a result, we would ask the Chamber to make a finding that there has been a violation of the "as soon as practicable," requirement of Rule 68, and to give us some remedy. And the only remedy that we can think of that would really help us at this stage is to give us time to review the material so that we would be in a position to use it with the upcoming witnesses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Irrespective of the conclusion the Chamber may reach, I'd like to explore the possibility with the parties of continuing the hearing with the second-next witness, who is -- forgive me for my pronunciation - Mulaoasmanovic, who was not affected by the disclosed material in question. So I would like to hear the parties of that possibility first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, speaking for our team, I'm not sure that we would be in a position to begin her cross-examination today. And also she's a person who was struck by a firing at a tram in Sarajevo, and I'm not sure whether any of this material would relate to military targets in that area or military personnel that may have been involved in transport on trams. But with that reservation, that's a possibility that we could entertain. The other possibility would be to go ahead with the testimony of Dr. Nakas, at the understanding that he can be recalled if it turns out there is material relating to the State Hospital, or perhaps the Prosecution is in a position to advise us at this point whether there's any material from the State Hospital that -- or in that vicinity that is on that material that we have not been given access to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Is she around, Mr. Tieger or Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour. My preliminary reaction is that that could well be a workable solution. If you'll forgive my caution, I would like to double-check on that and see if there are any logistical or other issues that I'm not aware of at the moment that might render that difficult or impossible. But as I say, the preliminary indication is that that would be a workable solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll adjourn for half an hour, and we'll --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can all hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume at 10 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We start in the open session, in the absence of the witness, to give our ruling. The Chamber has considered the arguments raised by the accused in the 17th Motion for Finding of Disclosure Violation and for Remedial Measures, as well as the oral submissions by the Prosecution and Mr. Robinson, for the accused, made this morning. According to the motion, the Prosecution disclosed 1.072 items, amounting to 5.740 pages, to the accused on 31st August 2010 as material which, I quote, "may fall within the ambit of Rule 68." This material was apparently seized by the Serbian MUP during searches conducted at two apartments in Belgrade and had been in the Prosecution's possession since January 2010. In the motion, the accused estimates that it would take him and his team a period of 12 working days to adequately review this new material, and requests an immediate suspension of proceedings to enable him to complete this exercise before the calling of further Prosecution witnesses. The Chamber will issue a decision in due course on whether or not the disclosure of this material in August of this year amounts to a violation of the Prosecution's obligations under Rule 68. Of more immediate concern is the question of whether a suspension of the proceedings is necessary to permit the accused to review it. The Chamber further recalls that an adjournment of the proceedings is an exceptional measure, which it will only order if convinced that it is in the interests of justice to do so. The Trial Chamber is satisfied that given the volume of material involved, the accused will require time to conduct a detailed review of these documents to determine whether they contain anything that is exculpatory or otherwise important for his defence. In light of Mr. Robinson's submission, the Trial Chamber is satisfied that the trial proceedings can continue today, with the hearing of the evidence of Bakir Nakas, and, subsequently, Alma Mulaosmanovic-Cehajic, and subject to the proviso that the accused may make a later application to recall them, showing good cause. However, the Chamber is convinced that it is in the interests of justice to suspend the proceedings, from the end of Mulaosmanovic's testimony, for a period of five days. As the parties were aware, we were already scheduled not to sit on Friday of this week and Monday and Tuesday of next week. We anticipate that Mulaosmanovic-Cehajic's testimony will conclude by the end of tomorrow and that we will, therefore, not sit on Wednesday, Thursday, or Friday of this week, and we will resume on Wednesday, 22nd September. That's the ruling by the Chamber, and we'll go into closed session again and we'll bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Also, with respect to the session that we had about -- discussion about this in closed session just prior to the recess, I would ask that the Chamber allow that it be part of the public transcript from page 39, line 16, until the end of that session. I don't think there was anything in any of our comments that would warrant that being in closed session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no opposition from your part, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: (redacted) I can't think of anything else, during the course of that submission, that was problematic. And assuming we are in closed session now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, we are in open session, Mr. Tieger, still in open session. So you are happy to lift the confidentiality of the previous debate, with the redaction of that part?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and also the redaction just of the reference just made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, then. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I wanted to raise a scheduling issue arising from the Court's ruling, and I wanted to respectfully, but strongly urge the Court, in addition to hearing the two witnesses specified, to also hear the testimony of Mr. Thomas. Mr. Thomas is a 67-year-old man who has just arrived from Canada. As matters stand, under the Court's guidance, should it turn out to be necessary, based on a review of the documentation, that he needs to be recalled, that can happen. But now we are in a position of sending him back, of ensuring that that would take place perhaps unnecessarily, when it need not happen. And I would also note my information is that Mr. Thomas, in any event, would not be available next week. But I think in the interests of both the witness and the Court's timing, I would strongly urge the Court to move forward on his testimony this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll consider your request. And do you have anything to respond, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly, Mr. President. But can we go into open session for this? It's not necessary to draw the blinds, but I think that this discussion should be held in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless we broadcast the witness, that should be okay. We'll go into open session briefly. And we also lift the confidentiality of the last part, in which Mr. Tieger stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, now we are in open session, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. President. I think we would agree that it's not necessary to inconvenience a witness if we have the right to recall the witness. And so if the Prosecution believes that it's in the best interests of the witness to give his testimony at this time, we can accommodate that, as far as we're concerned. I also wanted to raise another matter with the Chamber about the scheduling, and that is that Dr. Karadzic, himself, had planned, on those days off, to see his family, have them -- they've scheduled a visit here. He didn't see them in August because he was reading Mladic diaries and we devoted that entire recess to that, and so it would be difficult to use that time for the purpose of reviewing these materials, as much as we appreciate the indulgence of the Chamber in giving us some time. In addition, because that time had previously been scheduled to be off, we scheduled a trip for our investigator to assist Dr. Subotic in viewing the sites in Sarajevo, and have been making arrangements with the Bosnian government to try to do that, and so our investigator wouldn't be available, too. He would be the person who would be normally assisting Dr. Karadzic in reviewing this material, which is all in B/C/S, and so I can't be of any help to him on that. So we would ask that you consider adjusting the schedule so that the five days that we have to review the material commence beginning on next Wednesday, or at least don't include the period of time which you had previously granted us as time off. And we appreciate, again, the accommodation of the Trial Chamber, but we simply wouldn't be able to get the material reviewed during the period that you've suggested. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll consider the matter and come back to you. But before --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just one small caveat. I appreciate Mr. Robinson's remarks with respect to Mr. Thomas, but I would just have to note that it wouldn't be the right to recall the witness. It would be the opportunity to do so if circumstances warrant it. But thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As I made it clear, it is so when good cause would be shown. We'll adjourn for half an hour and resume at five past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we start in open session to discuss matters raised in the last session. Before that, I note that Ms. Sutherland joins us. Good afternoon, Ms. Sutherland. I was advised that you have something to raise, Mr. Karadzic, or was it Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It just relates to the cross-examination time for the next witness that Mr. Karadzic wanted to be heard on. I don't know if it's necessary to hear him now, but at some point before the next witness begins, he would like to be heard on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's high time -- it's the appropriate time to hear that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. Looking at the amalgamated statement by the next witness, we can see that it has 96 paragraphs. The witness quite loosely and arbitrarily makes some assessments which it is very easy to question if we are more specific. So if the intention of the Chamber is to give any kind of attention to his amalgamated statement, without authenticating medical documents, and if the statement is admitted, then I need at least two minutes per paragraph, plus the documents. So it is unacceptable for the Defence for documents to be admitted without testing what he says in the statement about the deployment of the artillery, what he saw at Hresa, and some other things. And the witness here knows how much it is possible to see Hresa from the Military Hospital. So if the statement is to be tendered and if the paragraphs are to be taken into consideration, then I would need at least two and maybe three minutes per paragraph in order to be able to be specific about what is in those paragraphs and what is not. So I would like you to take that into account. Otherwise, we can just disregard the statement and just take note or consider only what he says about the documents. Otherwise, we will be in the situation that these unsubstantiated, arbitrary statements counter quite serious and grounded statements by other serious witnesses. Then that would really be disproportional equality of arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, as was informed to you earlier on, the Chamber allowed you an hour to cross-examine that witness, it was based upon the following factors: Of course, the length of his amalgamated statement, which I remember of 35 pages, and the fact that the Prosecution will use only a quarter of an hour for its examination-in-chief, and, in particular, the limited scope of his testimony, and also the lack of specific evidence about you and your role. Moreover, you had a lengthy cross-examination of Dr. Milan Mandilovic, who provided similar testimony. So in light of these situations, the Chamber will not revisit the time for cross-examination of -- your cross-examination of Dr. Nakas. But as we indicated earlier on, it was not something which was set in stone, so as long as you remain efficient and relevant in your questioning. There's a possibility for you to get some addition time, but it depends upon your conduct of cross-examination. That said, we also, as was informed earlier on, that your cross-examination of the next witness, Ms. Mulaosmanovic, should be limited to one hour as well. And as for the Mr. Thomas, given the -- in light of the submissions from both parties, we -- before adjourning at all, we'll hear Mr. Thomas, after the two witnesses I referred to. In assessing what is a reasonable time for cross-examination, the Chamber has taken into account the following in relation to Mr. Thomas: The range of matters addressed in the witness's amalgamated statement, including the meetings with some members of the Serbian -- I beg your pardon, Sarajevo Romanija Corps and the ABiH; number 2, the fact that many of the documents tendered by the Prosecution as associated exhibits run only to one page and are not complex; number 3, the length of his testimony in Galic and Slobodan Milosevic, including the time taken in both cases for cross-examination; number 4, the time the witness was in Sarajevo, which is approximately nine months; and, finally, number 5, the fact that many of the issues covered by this witness have been dealt with by other witnesses, albeit at varyingly different time-frames; i.e., KDZ-185, Richard Mole, and van Lynden. On the basis of these factors, the Chamber agreed to allow you three hours for your cross-examination of this witness. That said, the Chamber is -- we think all the examinations of these three witnesses should be able to be concluded by the end of Wednesday this week and that -- I beg your pardon. Let me consult our agenda. Yes. We should be able to conclude the examination of these three witnesses by the end of Wednesday's sitting. And then, as was informed, we're not sitting on Thursday/Friday this week and also will not be sitting on -- and then we decided not to sit during the whole week next week. I hope that will give more than sufficient time to the accused to review all those materials. Unless there's anything further to be raised by the parties, we'll go into closed session. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When I ordered the order to lift the confidentiality of the transcript, I should have -- I should have meant to include the audio/video part as well. So that will be -- that part also will be lifted. Yes, we'll go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before we do, Mr. President, just thank you very much for your ruling, and I would just ask if the Chamber would allow itself and the parties to remain available on Thursday in the event that Dr. Karadzic is able to convince you to give him some additional time. I note particularly with Mr. Thomas, he was in Sarajevo for about one year, and I don't really think, with all due respect, that there's going to be any way that his cross-examination can be effectively completed within three hours. And perhaps when you see what Dr. Karadzic is doing, you might wish to give him some additional time. But it would be helpful if everyone could keep Thursday open so that in the event you do decide to give him additional time, we're able to do that without inconveniencing anybody. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Those two days were originally -- those were the days on which we were originally planning to sit. I take it there's no problem, but I encourage or require the accused to comply with the three hours' limit for his cross-examination. The witness is already in. We'll go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 14th day of September, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: [Closed session] [Confidentiality partially lifted by order of Chamber]
[Closed session] [Confidentiality partially lifted by order of Chamber]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.21 p.m.,
